A family loan can remain unpaid on paper while your own bill still needs cash

Separate the principal record from accessible cash, compare scheduled and delayed receipts, and test the lender’s own bill against a monthly cash ledger.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Stress the lender’s own bill before relying on scheduled repayments

Interactive planning lab

Cash immediately after the entered family advance$40,000
Extra initial cash needed to avoid a negative delayed-case ledger$4,000
Unpaid original principal at the end of the delayed-case window$13,000

Original interest-free family-loan cash illustration, not a contract, collection forecast or fair-value estimate. The principal leaves accessible cash at month zero. Scheduled principal receipts begin at the entered first repayment month and repeat monthly, capped at the unpaid principal; the delayed case shifts the entire receipt schedule by the entered delay. Repayment is a transfer from unpaid principal into cash, not additional interest income. Each month’s ordinary cash surplus and any repayment arrive before the lender’s separate bill is paid at that month-end. Negative ledger values show an unfunded amount, not an authorised overdraft or an automatically financed payment. Extra initial cash is the amount needed to lift the entire selected ledger to zero or above; it includes any underlying budget deficit as well as the loan’s timing effect. No interest, tax, fees, default probability, collateral, enforcement or assumed credit line is modeled. Unpaid principal is a nominal record of original principal not yet received, not proof of collectability or spendable wealth. Only events within the reporting window appear; an excluded later bill or repayment is not cancelled. The keep-cash control advances no family money and therefore does not provide the same assistance.

The central idea

A repayment promise does not fund a bill before the cash arrives. Track unpaid principal separately and test your own payment calendar under a delay.

01

Record the cash leaving before counting any future receipt

Lending money to a family member changes the lender’s immediate access to cash. A record of the amount still owed can help track the arrangement, but it cannot be used to pay another bill before the borrower actually repays it.

The example starts with CAD 60,000 of accessible cash. An interest-free advance of CAD 20,000 leaves at month zero, reducing that cash to CAD 40,000. The unpaid original principal record starts at CAD 20,000. The calculator keeps those two quantities separate and does not value the receivable as a liquid asset.

All amounts and dates are original assumptions. The tool assumes a repayable principal advance for its arithmetic; it does not decide whether a real transfer is legally a loan or a gift, assess collection rights or determine what the borrower can afford.

02

Put the lender’s separate commitments on the same calendar

The lender has an assumed CAD 500 monthly cash surplus after ordinary spending and a separate CAD 50,000 bill in month twelve. The surplus is not interest from the loan. It is other household cash left after routine costs and is the same in every comparison.

The original repayment schedule begins in month six, with CAD 1,000 of principal returned each month until the original advance is repaid. The model credits each month’s ordinary surplus and any principal receipt before paying the one-time bill at that month-end. A bill arriving earlier within the month could need another timing buffer.

The keep-cash control makes no family advance. It provides a useful reference for the lender’s cash, but it does not provide the same assistance to the family member. It should not be described as an equally supportive alternative merely because its cash line is higher.

03

Count only the repayments that arrive before the bill

Under the scheduled case, receipts occur in months six through twelve before the lender’s bill. That is seven payments, or CAD 7,000. By the end of month twelve, cash is CAD 40,000 after the advance, plus CAD 6,000 of ordinary surplus, plus CAD 7,000 received, less the CAD 50,000 bill: CAD 3,000.

Without the advance, the same cash calculation ends month twelve at CAD 16,000. The difference is not the full original CAD 20,000 because CAD 7,000 has already returned. The on-schedule loan still has CAD 13,000 of original principal unpaid at that point.

A principal repayment moves an amount from the unpaid-principal record into cash. It is not an additional investment gain on top of that principal. This illustration charges no interest and makes no tax calculation.

04

A delayed schedule can leave an earlier bill unfunded

The default stress shifts every repayment twelve months later, so the first receipt arrives in month eighteen. There are no principal receipts before the month-twelve bill. The lender’s ledger then becomes CAD 40,000 + CAD 6,000 − CAD 50,000 = minus CAD 4,000.

The negative number identifies an unfunded amount. It does not mean a bank has supplied an overdraft or that the bill has somehow been paid. To make every ledger date non-negative under this exact scenario, the lender would need CAD 4,000 of additional cash available at the start, or another explicitly modeled response.

Later receipts can improve the later balance but cannot retroactively fund the earlier payment date. A positive result at the end of a reporting window is therefore not enough to establish that the plan could be carried out throughout it.

05

Keep the ending principal record separate from collectability

At the end of the selected 24 months, the on-schedule case has received nineteen CAD 1,000 payments. It shows CAD 21,000 in the cash ledger and CAD 1,000 of unpaid principal. The delayed case has received seven payments and shows CAD 9,000 in its raw cash ledger with CAD 13,000 unpaid.

Those are cash-and-principal records under the stated receipt schedules. They do not establish the economic value of either remaining claim. An unpaid amount can be due later, disputed, partly recoverable or not recoverable; the model has no evidence from which to value those possibilities.

The delayed case’s CAD 9,000 ending ledger also does not erase the earlier CAD 4,000 funding gap. If CAD 4,000 were actually added at the beginning, it would change every cash point and the ending amount. The displayed ledger remains the unfinanced scenario, with the separate funding-need metric making that missing resource visible.

06

Test the lender’s deadline and the receipt delay together

The matrix changes the lender’s bill month and the delay applied to the original repayment schedule. Each cell calculates the extra starting cash needed over the whole selected window. It is not simply the cash balance on the bill date or the amount expected from the borrower at the end.

This distinction matters if the ordinary monthly surplus is negative or the advance itself exceeds starting cash. The lender can then need additional funds before the separate bill arrives. The bar comparison includes the keep-cash control so an underlying budget deficit is not silently attributed entirely to helping the family member.

A repayment amount of zero produces no receipts in the model, without treating the unpaid principal as forgiven. Likewise, a first receipt or bill after the reporting window remains outside the displayed dates; it is not cancelled. Review the window before concluding that an obligation has disappeared.

07

Use the calendar to make the arrangement specific

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s family-lending guidance asks people to clarify whether support is a gift or a loan, consider their own finances, and discuss repayment dates and changed circumstances. That U.S. educational source supports a conversation about expectations; it does not supply Canadian tax or legal treatment for this illustration.

  1. Separate money already committed to your own bills from cash available to advance.
  2. State the amount, first receipt date and repayment frequency clearly.
  3. Check your own payment calendar under an agreed delay stress.
  4. Keep actual receipts and unpaid principal in separate records.
  5. Revisit the plan when either household’s circumstances change.

No default probability, enforcement, collateral, interest, fee, tax, borrowing facility or promise of repayment is included. The purpose is to expose the lender’s cash dependence on future receipts, rather than to label a relative’s reliability or replace an actual agreement.
